clinicalPearls: A spectrum of autoimmune neurological disorders linked to high-titre antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase, the enzyme that synthesises the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA.
The core phenotypes are stiff-person syndrome, cerebellar ataxia, limbic and extralimbic encephalitis, and a form of drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy.
Stiff-person syndrome features axial and proximal rigidity with painful superimposed spasms, often triggered by startle, noise or emotion, and an exaggerated startle response.
Very high antibody titres, and especially detection in cerebrospinal fluid with intrathecal synthesis, distinguish the neurological syndrome from the low titres seen in ordinary type 1 diabetes.
Strong association with other organ-specific autoimmunity, notably type 1 diabetes mellitus, autoimmune thyroid disease and pernicious anaemia.
Because GAD is intracellular, the antibody may be a marker rather than directly pathogenic, and responses to immunotherapy are consequently variable and often partial.
First-line symptomatic treatment of stiff-person syndrome uses GABA-enhancing agents such as benzodiazepines and baclofen; immunotherapy is added for the neurological disease.
Consider a paraneoplastic search, particularly for thymoma or neuroendocrine tumours, when antibodies coexist with other onconeural markers or the course is atypical.
reference.pathophysiology: Glutamic acid decarboxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme converting glutamate to gamma-aminobutyric acid, the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter, and it is expressed both in inhibitory neurones of the central nervous system and in pancreatic islet beta cells, which explains the overlap with type 1 diabetes. In the neurological syndromes, high-titre antibodies target the GAD65 isoform, and impaired GABAergic inhibition is thought to underlie the clinical picture: reduced inhibitory tone in spinal and brainstem circuits produces the continuous motor unit activity, rigidity and spasms of stiff-person syndrome, while dysfunction of cerebellar Purkinje cells and hippocampal interneurones underlies the ataxic and epileptic-encephalitic phenotypes. Because the enzyme is intracellular, the antibodies cannot easily access their target in living neurones, so a purely antibody-mediated mechanism is debated and cytotoxic T-cell responses against GAD-expressing neurones are also implicated; this contrasts with disorders caused by antibodies to cell-surface synaptic proteins, which are directly pathogenic and more reliably reversible. The frequent coexistence of several organ-specific autoantibodies reflects a broader predisposition to autoimmunity, and the intracellular, partly T-cell-mediated nature of the process helps explain why neurological deficits often respond incompletely and can become fixed.
additionalDifferentials: Stiff-person syndrome from antibodies to glycine receptor or amphiphysin
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus
Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration from other onconeural antibodies
Autoimmune encephalitis due to surface antigen antibodies such as anti-LGI1 or anti-NMDA receptor
additionalInvestigations: Serum GAD65 antibody titre by radioimmunoassay or ELISA
Paired cerebrospinal fluid GAD antibodies with assessment of intrathecal synthesis
Electromyography showing continuous motor unit activity in agonist and antagonist muscles
MRI brain, including hippocampal sequences, for cerebellar atrophy or limbic signal change
Broader autoimmune encephalitis and paraneoplastic antibody panel
Screening for associated autoimmunity (thyroid antibodies, glucose and islet markers, B12)
Cross-sectional imaging for occult tumour, including thymus, when a paraneoplastic cause is suspected
redFlags: Truncal rigidity with spasms threatening ventilation or causing joint dislocation and fractures
Autonomic instability or crises with hyperthermia and blood pressure lability during severe spasms
Rapidly progressive encephalopathy, seizures or reduced consciousness suggesting encephalitis
Sudden falls without protective reflexes from startle-induced spasms
Features suggesting an underlying malignancy prompting urgent tumour search
reference.prognosis: Outcomes vary with phenotype: stiff-person syndrome is often chronic but partly controllable with symptomatic and immune therapy, whereas GAD-associated cerebellar ataxia and epilepsy frequently respond poorly and may progress to fixed disability. Early treatment offers the best chance of limiting permanent deficit.
pitfalls: Treating low GAD antibody titres, common in type 1 diabetes, as proof of a neurological syndrome
Dismissing stiff-person syndrome as functional or psychogenic because of its startle-related, emotionally modulated spasms
Withdrawing benzodiazepines abruptly, which can precipitate severe rigidity and autonomic crisis
Expecting the reliable reversibility seen with surface-antigen antibody encephalitis
Omitting a paraneoplastic and coexisting-autoimmunity work-up
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Consensus guidance on autoimmune and paraneoplastic neurological syndromes
management: Symptomatic GABA-enhancing therapy for stiff-person syndrome with benzodiazepines and baclofen to reduce rigidity and spasms
Immunotherapy with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, with variable and often partial response reflecting the intracellular target
Antiseizure medication for the associated drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy
Screen for and manage associated organ-specific autoimmunity including type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease and pernicious anaemia
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy for rigidity, gait and functional impairment
Multidisciplinary neurology follow-up, treating early to limit progression to fixed cerebellar or epileptic disability
